title: Being Judged by AI
hook: An algorithm may now screen your résumé, score your loan, or rank your rental application before any human sees it. Knowing that — and your rights — is the first step to a fair shot.
key_points: AI increasingly filters big decisions: hiring, lending, housing, insurance, benefits.
It can be faster and more consistent — but also opaque and biased.
A rejection may come from a model no human reviewed; bias can hide in the data.
Many places now grant rights: to know, to an explanation, and to a human review.
content_html: We usually talk about AI as a tool we use. But increasingly, AI is used on us — quietly making or shaping decisions that affect our lives before any person is involved. Apply for a job, and an automated system may scan and rank your résumé, with most applications filtered out before a human recruiter ever looks. Apply for a loan, a credit card, an apartment, insurance, or even some government benefits, and an algorithm may score your risk and effectively decide the outcome. These systems are attractive to organizations because they're fast, cheap, and consistent — they don't get tired or play favorites the way an individual might.
extra_html: The trouble is what they hide. An AI gatekeeper can be a black box: you're rejected, but no one — sometimes not even the company — can clearly explain why, and there may have been no human in the loop at all. Worse, these models learn from historical data, so they can quietly inherit and automate past discrimination — screening out qualified people based on patterns tied to gender, race, age, or zip code, all while appearing neutral and objective. Real cases have surfaced hiring tools that penalized women and lending models that disadvantaged minority applicants. The encouraging news is that the law is starting to respond. A growing number of places now give people rights when automated systems make significant decisions about them: the right to be told that AI was used, the right to an explanation, and the right to request a human review or appeal. The practical move if an important decision feels wrong is to ask directly whether an automated system was involved and whether you can have it reviewed by a person — and to know that, increasingly, you're entitled to.

related.title: Bias & Fairness
related.hook: AI learns from data made by people, so it inherits our patterns — including the unfair ones. A model trained on a biased past will confidently recommend a biased future.

related.title: Rules & Regulation
related.hook: AI raced ahead of the law, and governments are now scrambling to catch up. The big debate: how to curb real harms without strangling a genuinely useful technology.

related.title: AI & Jobs
related.hook: AI is less likely to take your whole job than to take certain tasks within it. The pattern through history: tools reshape work faster than they erase it.

related.title: AI Doesn't Just Inherit Bias — It Invents New Ones
related.hook: A hiring simulation found ChatGPT, Claude, and Gemini turned one failed candidate into a stereotype for their whole group — segregating candidates far more aggressively than human participants did.

flashcards.prompt: What's a key risk when AI screens job or loan applications?

choices.text: Hidden bias and opaque rejections no human reviewed
It can only reject, never approve

flashcards.explanation_html: Automated gatekeeping can be biased (inheriting it from data) and opaque — you may be filtered out by a model without a human ever seeing your case.

flashcards.prompt: If an automated decision affects you, what rights might you have?
flashcards.back_html: In many places: to be told AI was used, to an explanation, and to request a human review or appeal. Rules vary, so it's worth asking.
